segments.text: In this video we are looking at how fast
API handles HTTP headers and cookies.
Every web request carries metadata
beyond the URL, things like
authentication tokens, language
preferences, and session identifiers.
Fast API gives you a clean declarative
way to read all of that and to write
cookies back to the client without
reaching into the raw request object by
hand.
Without a framework helping you, reading
a header like authorization or accept
language means writing something like
request.headers.get,
passing in an exact string key, and
handling the case where it is missing
yourself. Do the same for cookies, and
you are now juggling two separate raw
dictionaries. There is no validation, no
documentation, and plenty of room for a
typo to cause a silent bug.
Here is a way to picture it. When a
letter arrives at a hotel front desk,
the staff do not hand the guest the
entire postal system. They read the
envelope, pull out the relevant
information, and pass it along in a
useful form. Fast API does exactly that
for your function. It inspects the
incoming HTTP envelope, extracts the
header or cookie you declared, validates
it, and injects it as a named parameter.
Fast API extends its dependency
injection style to headers and cookies
through two special classes, header and
cookie. You use them as default values
on your function parameters, exactly
like query or path. When a request
arrives, Fast API knows to look in the
right part of the HTTP message for each
one. The underscore to hyphen mapping is
a small but important detail, because
Python identifiers cannot contain
hyphens, writing accept_language
automatically targets the accept
language header.
Starting at the top, we import Fast API,
then header and cookie from fastapi, and
JSONResponse for the login route.
In get_profile, the parameter
authorization uses header with a default
of none. Fast API I will look for the
authorization header and inject whatever
it finds, or none if it is absent.
The parameter authorization header
accept_language maps automatically to
the accept language header because
FastAPI converts underscores to hyphens.
The session_id parameter uses cookie, so
FastAPI looks in the cookie jar of the
incoming request instead. In the login
route, we build a JSON response
manually, then call set_cookie on it to
attach a set cookie header to the
outgoing response, marking it HTTP only,
so JavaScript cannot read it.
When a request arrives, FastAPI's
dependency resolution layer examines
each parameter default before your
function is called. For header, it
converts the Python name to a hyphenated
key and looks it up in the request
headers dictionary. For cookie, it uses
the name as is against the past cookie
store. If a required header or a cookie
is missing, FastAPI returns a 422
Unprocessable Entity response with a
clear error message. You do not write
that error handling yourself. As a
bonus, all declared headers and cookies
are included in the OpenAPI schema
FastAPI generates.
Header and cookie shine when you know
exactly which values you need, and you
want FastAPI to validate and document
them for you.
They are a natural fit for reading an
auth token, a language preference, or a
session identifier. However, if your
security logic is complex, FastAPI's
OAuth2 and HTTP bearer security schemes
are a better starting point. If you need
to read every header that arrives, say
to proxy them wholesale, just use the
raw request.headers object directly
rather than declaring dozens of
individual parameters.
To wrap up, header and cookie follow the
same declarative pattern as query and
path, so there is very little new syntax
to learn. The underscore to hyphen
conversion handles the one naming
mismatch between Python and HTTP.
Validation and error responses are
automatic, and your declared parameters
appear in the open API docs. When you
need to write a cookie back, build or
inject a response object and call set
underscore cookie on it before
returning.
